analysis.one_liner: Repeals the federal estate, gift, and generation-skipping transfer taxes on large inheritances.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee hearing or a floor vote and died when the 111th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would wipe out the federal taxes on very large transfers of wealth: the estate tax owed when someone dies, the gift tax owed on large lifetime gifts, and the tax on transfers that skip a generation. These taxes touch only the largest estates and gifts, so the tax cut would go almost entirely to the wealthiest households, while the federal government would lose the revenue those taxes raise.
analysis.who_benefits: The wealthiest families holding large estates and planning large lifetime gifts. The estate tax applies only to estates above a multi-million-dollar exemption, so repeal's benefits concentrate at the very top; the biggest savings go to the biggest fortunes.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Very wealthy families with large estates

how_it_helps.text: The bill repeals the entire subtitle of the tax code covering estate, gift, and generation-skipping transfer taxes, applying to deaths and gifts after enactment.

Because the estate tax only applies above a large exemption amount, repeal directs its savings to the largest inheritances, and repealing the gift tax along with it would also let large wealth be transferred during life free of federal tax.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers generally. The revenue these taxes raise would disappear, leaving the choice of larger deficits or higher other taxes to make up for it.

drawbacks.text: Repeal eliminates the main federal tax on inherited wealth, so the largest fortunes would pass to heirs entirely untaxed, while the lost revenue would have to be replaced by borrowing or by taxing other income.

Repealing the gift tax at the same time would remove the backstop that keeps wealthy people from simply giving away assets during life to avoid estate tax, making avoidance even easier than under estate-tax repeal alone.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is a concentrated tax cut for a small number of the largest estates; the cost is lost federal revenue borne broadly. Very large family farms and businesses gain some relief, but the exemption levels already shielded most estates, so the overwhelming share of the benefit flows to the biggest fortunes.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never acted on it, and it died there when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Mac Thornberry introduced the Death Tax Repeal Act on January 6, 2009, with 17 original cosponsors, and it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day.
The bill would repeal the federal estate, gift, and generation-skipping transfer taxes.
Ninety-four House Republicans cosponsored the bill, but the Ways and Means Committee took no further action, and the bill's last action in the record is the committee referral.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, the estate and gift taxes continued to apply to large inheritances and gifts, preserving that revenue for the general budget rather than directing it to the heirs of the largest estates.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: General taxpayers; large estates stayed taxed

for.name: Rep. Mac Thornberry
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the estate, gift, and generation-skipping transfer taxes and referred it to Ways and Means.

against.name: Rep. Charlie Rangel
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a committee markup or a hearing; it sat without action after referral.

sides.party_line_note: All 94 cosponsors were Republicans; no Democrat cosponsored, and the bill never advanced past the Democratic-controlled committee.

industries.note: Repeal would spare the largest estates and gifts from federal transfer tax entirely, with savings concentrated at the very top of the wealth distribution. The lost revenue would otherwise be available for public purposes or deficit reduction.
A full repeal would eliminate much of the planning work built around estate and gift taxes. This is a small effect compared with the main fiscal shift.
